summary: Research-grounded design brief for a CITS1401 (UWA) beginner Python practice app. Key evidence: novices' hardest and most-repeated mistakes are semantic/conceptual, not syntactic (Brown & Altadmri 2015; Ettles/Luxton-Reilly/Denny 2018), so detection and reporting should weight repeated logic misconceptions and time-to-fix over first-time syntax slips. Skills develop in a rough hierarchy tracing -> reading/explaining -> writing (Lister 2004; Lopez 2008; Xie 2019), so each topic should ladder formats: predict-output/trace table -> Parsons/fix-the-bug -> write-a-function. Parsons problems give the same learning in far less time (Ericson 2017/2018; ITiCSE WG 2022/23), paired distractors and intra-problem adaptation are recommended. Hints should be tiered, dwell-gated and logged, because hint-abuse (viewing 68% of hint levels for <1 s; gaming the system costs ~1/3 of learning) is a strong negative signal (Aleven; Baker et al.); explanations plus self-explanation prompts are what make hints transfer (Marwan et al. 2019). Mastery gating helps weaker students; spaced, interleaved retrieval scheduled per TOPIC with daily credit raised exam grades ~1%/hour (YeckehZaare, Resnick & Ericson 2019). Technically: run real CPython 3.12 in the browser via Pyodide in a Web Worker (worker.terminate() for infinite loops, setStdin for input(), the 'ast' module for static misconception checks, 3.10-3.12 'Did you mean' messages for free), edit in Monaco (pin 0.52.x AMD build from cdnjs) for the VS Code feel. Deliverables 1-7 below are each a finding with detection channels, formats, hint tiers, difficulty rubric, unlock/review rules, report design, and extras, plus a topic ladder aligned to CITS1401 and UWA 2026 teaching weeks.

findings.topic: 0. Research base - what the literature says novices get wrong and why
findings.detail: Qian & Lehman (2017, ACM TOCE) organise novice difficulties into SYNTACTIC (colons, indentation, brackets), CONCEPTUAL (wrong notional-machine model: assignment, loops, scope, return) and STRATEGIC (cannot plan/decompose, cannot test) knowledge; many misconceptions come from transfer of natural-language/maths meaning (e.g. '=' as equality, 'while' as continuous monitoring). Brown & Altadmri (SIGCSE 2015, 37M compilations, 250k students): the single most frequent mistake was unbalanced brackets (syntax) but it had a median time-to-fix of 17 s and students learned to avoid it by mid-term; semantic/type mistakes were more frequent in aggregate, were REPEATED by the same student (~4x each for string-== and ignored-return-value), and the ones producing no error had median time-to-fix >= 1000 s (cap). Conclusion: report on repetition and time-to-fix, and weight semantic errors above syntax. Ettles, Luxton-Reilly & Denny (ACE 2018, 15,000 fragments): logic errors split into algorithmic errors, misinterpretation of the problem, and fundamental misconceptions; misconceptions were the most frequent and hardest to resolve. Kohn (2019) on >4000 high-school Python programs: a large fraction of errors are misspellings/superficial; Kohn & Manaris (SIGCSE 2020, TigerJython): ~1/3 of syntax-error instances were 'superficial' (missing colon, misspelt keyword) and 95% were fixed immediately once the message was clear; return-vs-print was the hardest concept they observed. Sorva (2013): the notional machine must be an explicit learning objective; Pea (1986) 'superbug' = students assume the computer understands intent. Catalogue entries at progmiscon.org relevant to CITS1401: AssignCompares ('=' compares), VariablesHoldExpressions ('=' stores the expression), AssignmentCopiesObject, IfIsLoop (if body repeats while condition holds), ConditionalIsSequence (if-else == two ifs), DeferredReturn (return does not exit immediately), ComparisonWithBoolLiteral, NoShortCircuit, MapToBooleanWithIf. Skill hierarchy: Lister et al. 2004 and Lopez et al. 2008 found tracing precedes reading/explaining which precedes writing; Xie et al. 2019 teach four skills in order (tracing, writing syntax, comprehending templates, writing with templates) and saw higher completion and lower error rates; Cunningham et al. 2017: students who sketch a trace succeed more on loop/array reading problems. 'Explain in plain English' ability correlates with code-writing ability (Murphy, Fitzgerald, Lister et al.). Metacognition: Prather et al. 2018/2019 found the most common failure is not building a correct model of the problem before coding; Loksa & Ko (CHI 2016) six stages (reinterpret prompt, search analogous problems, search solutions, evaluate, implement, evaluate implementation).

findings.topic: 1. Mistake taxonomy with detection channels (4 channels available in a browser app)
findings.detail:
DETECTION CHANNELS: (R) Runtime: Pyodide raises real CPython 3.12 exceptions - capture type, message, line number from the traceback, plus 3.10-3.12 'Did you mean ...?' suggestions and SyntaxWarnings; also worker timeout and 'function returned None but printed X'. (S) Static: run Python's own 'ast' module inside Pyodide on the student's code (no regex fragility) plus 'compile()' for precise SyntaxError text; a handful of regexes for pre-parse checks. (D) MCQ distractor: every wrong option carries a 'mistake' id so choosing it logs the misconception. (T) Hidden-test signature: each hidden test is tagged with the mistake it exposes (empty list, boundary index, float expected, call-twice). Each mistake id also carries category (syntax/conceptual/strategic) for the report.

TAXONOMY (id | topic | category | detection):
1 indent_error | if/else | syntax | R: IndentationError 'expected an indented block after if statement on line N', 'unexpected indent', 'unindent does not match any outer indentation level', TabError. S: regex mixed tabs/spaces; line ending in ':' not followed by deeper indent. D: predict-output distractor that treats a dedented line as inside the block.
2 missing_colon | if/loops/def | syntax | R: SyntaxError 'expected \':\'' (3.10+). S: regex ^\s*(if|elif|else|for|while|def|try|except|finally|with)\b.*[^:]\s*$ (skip lines with open brackets).
3 assign_vs_compare | if/else | conceptual | R: SyntaxError 'invalid syntax. Maybe you meant == or := instead of =?' for 'if x = 5:'. S: ast.Expr whose value is ast.Compare at statement level ('x == 5' meant as assignment, silently does nothing). D: 'AssignCompares' distractor ('= checks whether they are equal').
4 off_by_one_range | for loops/lists | conceptual | R: none (or IndexError when range(len(x)+1)). S: ast Call range with args (1, len(x)), (len(x)+1), (0, n-1) compared with spec metadata; T: boundary tests (first/last element, n=0); trace-table: student writes one extra/fewer row; D: distractor that includes the stop value.
5 int_vs_float_division | variables/expressions | conceptual | R: TypeError 'list indices must be integers or slices, not float' (used / result as index). S: ast BinOp FloorDiv where spec expects average; 'int(a/b)' with negatives. T: test expecting 2.5 receives 2 or vice versa. D: '7/2 == 3'.
6 string_immutability | strings | conceptual | R: TypeError 'str object does not support item assignment' (same for tuple). S: ast.Expr statement whose value is Call to str method returning new value (upper/lower/replace/strip/title) -> 'result discarded'. T: output unchanged.
7 mutate_while_iterating | lists/dicts | conceptual | R: RuntimeError 'dictionary changed size during iteration' (dicts only; lists silently skip). S: inside ast.For over Name X, a Call X.remove/pop/insert/append or Delete X[...]. T: list with adjacent matches [1,2,2,3] -> one survivor.
8 print_vs_return | functions | conceptual | R/T: harness sees return value None while captured stdout equals the expected value -> targeted message; 'return print(x)'. S: ast.FunctionDef with no ast.Return but calls print when task says 'return'. D: 'x = f(3) makes x equal 5' when f only prints. Kohn & Manaris and Kallia & Sentance flag this as the hardest concept.
9 forgot_to_call | functions | syntax/conceptual | R: TypeError "'<' not supported between instances of 'function' and 'int'"; stdout contains '<function '. S: ast.Expr that is a bare Name bound to a FunctionDef; Compare with a function Name.
10 shadow_builtin | variables/lists | strategic | S: assignment/For-target/parameter names in {list,str,sum,max,min,len,input,print,dict,int,float,type,id,range,sorted,next,map,filter,set,tuple,any,all}. R: TypeError "'list' object is not callable" / "'int' object is not callable" (message names the shadowed type). Report as PEP 8 / best-practice warning, not failure.
11 mutable_default_arg | functions | conceptual | S: ast.FunctionDef defaults containing ast.List/ast.Dict/ast.Set or Call(list/dict). T: call the function twice, expect independent results.
12 scope_confusion | functions | conceptual | R: UnboundLocalError "cannot access local variable 'total' where it is not associated with a value" (3.11 wording), NameError for a function-local read at module level. S: Name assigned inside a FunctionDef that also exists at module level with no 'global' (student expects the function to change the outer variable); Name read after the call that was only ever assigned inside the function. D: 'the function changes the global count'.
13 input_without_int | variables/input | conceptual | R: TypeError "'<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'", "can only concatenate str (not 'int') to str"; silent wrong result ('3'+'4' -> '34', '5'*3). S: Name assigned from input() later used in BinOp/Compare with a numeric Constant without int()/float(). D: predict-output distractor '7' for input()+input(). Also ValueError 'invalid literal for int() with base 10' -> validation lesson.
14 infinite_while | while loops | conceptual | R: worker timeout (e.g. 3 s) -> terminate + message 'your loop never finished; which variable should change?'; optional sys.settrace step cap gives the line. S: ast.While whose test Names are never assigned in the body and no ast.Break; 'while True' without break. Trace-table: student cannot finish the table.
15 is_vs_equals | if/else | conceptual | R: SyntaxWarning '"is" with int literal. Did you mean "=="?' (3.8+) - enable warnings capture. S: ast.Compare with Is/IsNot where a side is a Constant other than None/True/False. D: distractor.
16 modify_loop_var | for loops | conceptual | S: assignment/AugAssign to the ast.For target inside the body. Trace table exposes the 'i = 2,5,8' belief. D: predict-output distractor.
17 dict_keyerror | dictionaries | conceptual/strategic | R: KeyError: 'banana' (key in message). S: Subscript store/aug-assign d[k] += 1 inside loop with no prior 'k in d' / .get / setdefault. T: unseen key test. Recommend dict.get(k, 0).
18 index_out_of_range | lists/strings | conceptual | R: IndexError 'list index out of range' / 'string index out of range'. S: x[len(x)]; range(len(x)+1) or range(1, len(x)+1) used for indexing. T: empty list, single element.
19 accumulator_init | while/for loops | conceptual/strategic | R: NameError "name 'total' is not defined" (never initialised) or UnboundLocalError. S: accumulator Name assigned with a Constant inside the loop body AND aug-assigned in the same body (reset every iteration); product initialised 0; max initialised 0. T: all-negative list for max, empty list. Trace table: wrong row 0.
EXTRA IDS worth including (high frequency in the literature): str_int_concat (print('Total: ' + total) -> TypeError; R), name_typo (NameError with 'Did you mean' - Kohn: misspellings are a large fraction; R, count separately as 'slips'), print_no_parens (SyntaxError 'Missing parentheses in call to print'; R), unclosed_bracket (SyntaxError "'(' was never closed"; R), or_with_literal ('if x == 1 or 2' - S: BoolOp with Constant operand), elif_vs_if (ConditionalIsSequence; T/D), compare_to_true ('if flag == True'; S, style), none_from_inplace ('x = lst.sort()' / 'x = lst.append(3)' -> later TypeError 'NoneType ...'; S: Assign whose value is Call to sort/append/extend/reverse), missing_base_case (RecursionError 'maximum recursion depth exceeded'; R), file_newline (forgot .strip() -> '\n' in values; T), file_not_closed (S: open() without with; style), tuple_immutability (R), zero_division (R). Log each occurrence as {mistakeId, channel, qid, ts, fixedAfterMs}; the report treats R/S detections during a write task as one 'occurrence' per run, and computes time-to-fix as time from first detection to the next passing run (Brown & Altadmri metric).

findings.topic: 2. Question-format catalogue: when each is best and how to autograde
findings.detail:
Ladder inside every topic (Lister/Lopez/Xie hierarchy, PRIMM Predict-Run-Investigate-Modify-Make): READ (predict-output, trace table, which-line-raises, code-reading MCQ) -> ASSEMBLE/REPAIR (cloze, Parsons, fix-the-bug) -> WRITE (write-a-function, refactor-to-idiom, test-writer).

MCQ (single best answer, 4 options, each distractor tagged with a mistake id): best for conceptual checks and cheap spaced retrieval; autograde by option id; show explanation for the chosen distractor, not just the right answer. One submit only (prevents trial-and-error gaming).
PREDICT-THE-OUTPUT: best on first exposure to a construct and for notional-machine misconceptions (IfIsLoop, DeferredReturn, off-by-one); autograde by normalised stdout compare (rstrip lines, normalise line endings, optional float tolerance); the expected output is computed by running the reference snippet in Pyodide at load time so authors never hand-type outputs; offer an MCQ variant with misconception-derived distractors for easy tier and free-text for medium.
TRACE TABLE (variables x iterations): best for while/for accumulators, nested loops, swaps; the student fills cells; expected table generated automatically by running the reference code under sys.settrace in Pyodide and snapshotting locals at the loop-header line; autograde per cell with partial credit; cell-level diagnostics (wrong last row -> off_by_one_range; wrong row 0 -> accumulator_init; extra row -> loop-exit misconception). Cunningham 2017 and Sorva's visual program simulation support this.
WHICH LINE RAISES / WHICH EXCEPTION: two-step (pick line, pick exception type); autograde by line number and type; best for error-message literacy (Becker et al.; ITiCSE 2019 WG) and for the 'explain this error' panel to pay off.
FIX-THE-BUG: buggy code + visible examples + hidden tests; autograde by running hidden tests; also compute line-diff vs original and reward minimal fixes (<= 2 lines changed) so students do not rewrite from scratch; bug carries a mistake id so failure logs it. Ericson et al. place fixing between Parsons and writing in difficulty/time.
FILL-IN-THE-BLANK (cloze, 1-3 blanks): best for Xie's 'writing syntax' skill and for isolating a single decision (range bounds, comparison operator, accumulator init); autograde by substituting blanks into the template and running hidden tests (accepts equivalent answers like 'i < len(x)' vs 'i <= len(x)-1'), with token-compare as the fallback for non-runnable cases.
PARSONS (drag to reorder, with indentation = 2D Parsons): best for medium algorithm structure before writing; same learning as writing in less time (Ericson, Margulieux & Rick 2017; Ericson et al. 2018); use PAIRED distractors (a correct line paired with a subtly wrong twin, e.g. range(len(x)) vs range(1,len(x))) per ITiCSE WG 2022/23; autograde by executing the assembled code against tests (allows alternative valid orders) with solution-order compare as fallback; intra-problem adaptation: after 2 failed attempts remove one distractor or lock the first line; keep 5-9 lines for beginners, 2D indentation only at medium/hard.
WRITE-A-FUNCTION WITH HIDDEN TESTS: capstone; autograde by calling the function in Pyodide with each test's args and comparing repr/equality (float tolerance 1e-6), plus stdin/stdout PROGRAM tasks (CITS1401 projects are program-style) using pyodide.setStdin with pre-supplied lines; each hidden test tagged with the mistake it exposes; also run the static ast checks (shadowing, mutable default, print-vs-return) and show them as warnings even when tests pass.
CODE-READING COMPREHENSION (EiPE-lite): 'Which sentence best describes what this function does?' with SOLO-graded distractors (line-by-line multistructural description vs the relational purpose - Zilles et al. rubric); autogradable as MCQ; the free-text EiPE version is not autogradable offline, so offer it as self-check with model answer and self-rating (stored as a confidence signal).
REFACTOR-TO-IDIOM: working but clunky code (index loop -> for-each/enumerate; if x == True; manual counting -> dict.get; nested if -> guard clause/early return; repeated ifs -> elif); autograde: hidden tests still pass AND ast check that the anti-pattern is gone / target idiom present; feeds the best-practices report. Hard tier only; keep list comprehensions optional.
PROPOSED CREATIVE FORMATS: (a) SPOT-THE-DIFFERENCE TWINS - two near-identical snippets differing in one token (/ vs //, return inside vs after loop, range(n) vs range(1,n)); student says whether outputs differ and predicts both; isolates exactly one misconception; autograde. (b) ERROR-MESSAGE TRANSLATOR - show a real traceback; pick the cause (MCQ) then the fixing line; autograde; trains the skill the ITiCSE WG says novices lack. (c) TEST-WRITER - given a spec and a secretly buggy implementation, the student supplies an input that exposes the bug; the app runs reference vs buggy on that input and checks they differ; autogradable; teaches edge cases (strategic knowledge, which Qian & Lehman say is under-taught). (d) RESTATE-THEN-WRITE - hard write tasks require one typed sentence restating the problem first (Prather; Loksa & Ko); not graded, shown next to the solution afterwards. (e) LIVE-EXPRESSION CHALLENGE in the scratchpad ('make this evaluate to 7 using //'); autograde by evaluating.
Authoring format suggestion (extends the SQL-hub schema): {id, topic, scenario, format, diff, concepts:[], mistakes:[], core:bool, week:n, prompt, code, options?, answer?, tests:[{args|stdin, expect, tag}], hints:[l1,l2,l3], solution, explanation}.

findings.topic: 3. Tiered hints, reveal rules, and hint usage as a signal
findings.detail: TIERS: L1 NUDGE - points at the concept or line without saying what to change ('Look at the first value total has before the loop'); for runtime errors L1 can be auto-generated from the exception->mistake mapping (the same text as the explain-this-error panel). L2 STRATEGY - a subgoal-labelled plan (Margulieux, Catrambone & Guzdial: 'initialise accumulator / update inside loop / use after loop'), still no code. L3 PARTIAL CODE - skeleton with blanks or first lines, or for Parsons lock the first line/remove a distractor (intra-problem adaptation). L4 FULL SOLUTION - annotated line by line, followed by a one-question self-explanation prompt ('Why is total initialised to 0 and not 1?') because Marwan, Price et al. (ICER 2019) found code hints with explanations improved immediate performance but only transferred when combined with self-explanation prompts. GATING (based on Aleven et al. finding 68% of pre-final hint levels viewed for <1 s, and Baker et al. finding gaming-the-system students learn ~2/3 as much): hints are on-demand only; L1 available after the first submit or 60 s; each further tier requires >= 1 more attempt or >= 30 s dwell on the previous tier; L4 requires >= 2 failed attempts or an explicit 'Show solution' confirm. REVEAL RULES BY FORMAT: MCQ and code-reading - reveal answer and explanation immediately after the single submit (no second guess); predict-output and trace table - 2 attempts then reveal with a step-through; Parsons/cloze/fix - 3 attempts, adaptive simplification at attempt 2; write-a-function - unlimited runs against visible examples, hidden-test results shown as pass/fail with the tag of the failing test's mistake ('fails on an empty list'), solution on request after 2 hidden-test failures. After L4 on any question, the question is marked 'seen', the student is offered a parameterised variant (random numbers/lists, expected output computed by running the reference), and the item goes into the spaced-review queue. RECORDING (per attempt record): hintTier (max tier viewed), hintTimestamps, attemptsBeforeFirstHint, msPerTier (detect <2 s skims), solvedAfterHint, revealedSolution. SCORING: credit 1.0 no hint, 0.9 L1, 0.75 L2, 0.5 L3, 0 L4 (counts as practised, not mastered). SIGNALS FOR THE REPORT: hint-dependence per topic (share of correct answers needing L3+), skim rate (tier views <2 s), help-avoidance (>3 wrong attempts and > 3x expected time with no hint - Aleven's 'help avoidance'), and bottom-out rate; these predict learning gains as strongly as error counts in tutoring-system research.

findings.topic: 4. Difficulty rubric and where tags live
findings.detail: CRITERIA (score each; easy = 0-1 criteria met, medium = 2-3, hard = 4+): (1) concepts combined >1 (loop + condition; list + function); (2) nesting depth >= 1 (loop in loop, if in loop with accumulator); (3) code length: easy <= 8 lines, medium 8-20, hard > 20 or multi-function; (4) hidden edge case not stated in the prompt (empty input, boundary, negative, duplicate); (5) requires decomposition or choosing a data structure; (6) tracing more than ~4 iterations or two variables changing together; (7) program-level I/O (stdin/stdout or file) rather than a single function; (8) the target mistake is 'strategic' rather than syntax/conceptual; (9) expected time: easy <= 2 min, medium 2-6, hard 6-15. Xie's template idea gives a clean line: easy = one canonical template used as taught; medium = template with one variation; hard = novel combination of templates. FORMAT DEFAULTS: MCQ/predict/cloze mostly easy-medium; trace/Parsons/fix mostly medium; write/refactor/test-writer medium-hard; a hard MCQ is allowed (e.g. aliasing or scope) but must be justified by criteria 1/6/8. TAG PLACEMENT: keep 'diff' PER QUESTION (matches the SQL-hub schema and lets the report break down by difficulty); a SCENARIO is a narrative wrapper ('Library fines', 'Unit marks file') holding a 3-6 question ladder, and its displayed difficulty is DERIVED (min-max of its questions) rather than authored, so authors never keep two tags in sync. Also tag per question: format, concepts[], mistakes[] (which ids it can detect), core (counts toward unlock), week (CITS1401 alignment), expectedSec. Filters on the topic page: difficulty chips (as in the SQL hub), format chips, and 'weak spots first' ordering driven by the report.
findings.source: https://www.benjixie.com/publication/cse-2019/ ; https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3077618 ; precedent: sql-practice-hub question schema {id, diff, topic, ...}

findings.topic: 5. Mastery, unlocking, skip path, and spaced review
findings.detail: UNLOCK RULE (fair and transparent): topic N+1 unlocks when (a) every 'core' question in topic N has been attempted, (b) hint-weighted mastery over core questions >= 70%, and (c) at least one ASSEMBLE/REPAIR item (Parsons or fix) and one WRITE item are solved - ensures the student has climbed the tracing->writing ladder rather than passing on MCQs alone. Mastery learning had a significant positive effect, especially for weaker students, when adopted for a Python course (NTNU/Excited). Show the rule on the locked card ('3 of 6 core done - 58% - need 70%'). Never lock the topic's description or cheat-sheet - only its questions. SKIP PATH for confident students: 'Test out' = 5 mixed questions from the topic's medium/hard pool (1 predict, 1 trace, 1 fix, 1 write, 1 MCQ), no hints, pass >= 4/5 -> unlock and mark the topic 'tested out' (distinct badge; the report notes it was not practised). Also a settings toggle 'Unlock everything' recording override:true - a self-directed university student should not be held hostage by a UI; it is logged so the report can caveat. RECOMMENDED LADDER for CITS1401 (course lecture order is: intro/variables and simple loops -> maths -> if/elif/else -> strings -> lists -> text files -> decisions and exceptions -> functions -> lists/tuples to dictionaries -> while loops/simulation -> search and recursion): 1 Variables, types and expressions (input/print, int/float/str, // and %, f-strings); 2 If/elif/else and booleans; 3 While loops (counters, sentinels, accumulators); 4 Strings (indexing, slicing, immutability, methods); 5 For loops and range; 6 Lists (mutation vs new list, aliasing, accumulators); 7 Functions (parameters, return vs print, scope, defaults, testing); 8 Dictionaries and tuples; 9 Files and exceptions (with open, strip/split, try/except, ValueError); 10 Putting it together (nested data, searching, simple simulation, recursion intro). This keeps the user's requested 'easy if/else -> harder functions/for loops' feel while matching the unit. SPACED REVIEW (YeckehZaare, Resnick & Ericson, ICER 2019: schedule TOPICS not questions, give credit per day for a minimum number of questions, show the evolving schedule; each hour of use was associated with +1.04% final exam grade; 32% of 193 students exceeded the required 45 days voluntarily): after a topic reaches mastery on day 0, schedule reviews at +2, +7, +21 days; a review = 3 questions from that topic not seen in the last 14 days, preferring formats the student was weakest in; score < 2/3 resets the interval to +2 and flags the topic in the report; sessions INTERLEAVE 2-3 due topics; landing page shows a 'Warm-up: 3 due questions' card and a small calendar strip of upcoming reviews. Mastery never re-locks, but the topic card shows a freshness ring that fades when a review is overdue.

findings.topic: 6. Report design and generating recommended patterns from the data
findings.detail: DATA MODEL (pure log -> derived views, like the SQL hub's attempts array): localStorage 'pp_attempts' = append-only records {ts, sessionId, qid, topic, format, diff, correct, score, attempts, hintTier, hintSkims, timeMs, expectedSec, mistakes:[ids], errorType, distractorId, mode:'practice'|'exam'|'review'|'testout'}; 'pp_sessions' = {id, start, end, count, correct, hints}; 'pp_topics' = cached mastery {mastery, freshness, unlockedAt, testedOut, override}; 'pp_mistakes' = {id: {count, lastTs, medianFixMs, qids}}; sessionStorage for the live timer; export/import JSON button (cap attempts at ~3000, oldest pruned). REPORT PAGE SECTIONS: (1) Topic heatmap - mastery %, attempts, hint-weighted score, freshness; STRONG = >= 85% with <= L1 hints on >= 5 items; WEAK = < 60%, or hint-dependence > 50%, or the same mistake id >= 3 times. (2) Mistake categories - bar per mistake id grouped syntax / conceptual / strategic, with REPEAT count and median time-to-fix (Brown & Altadmri: repetition and slow fixes, not first occurrence, mark real difficulty); syntax slips (typos, colons) shown de-emphasised. (3) Format x topic matrix - accuracy by format reveals where on the tracing->reading->writing ladder the student sits; generate a sentence, e.g. 'You trace loops well (90%) but writing them lands at 40% - practise Parsons then write tasks in Topic 5'. (4) Trend over sessions - sparkline of accuracy, hint rate and minutes per session; session list with date, duration, items, new mistake ids. (5) Time-on-task - median time per format vs the question's expectedSec; flag RUSHED (< 25% expected and wrong -> guessing) and STUCK (> 3x expected with no hint -> help avoidance). (6) Exam readiness - performance in exam-mode sessions only (no hints, timed), by topic. RECOMMENDED PATTERNS GENERATOR (rule-based, no AI needed): a catalogue of ~20 'pattern cards' {id, title, bad snippet, good snippet, why, reference (PEP 8 section / Python docs), triggers:[mistake ids or ast flags]}; a card is recommended when its trigger count >= 2 in the last 14 days or a refactor question with that target failed; a card is shown as 'already using' when the ast scan of passing submissions finds the idiom (enumerate, with open, dict.get, f-strings, early return). Card list: snake_case names and 4-space indent (PEP 8); do not shadow built-ins; 'for item in items' instead of range(len(items)); enumerate when you need the index; 'in' for membership; dict.get(k, 0) / 'if k in d' before indexing; 'with open(...)' and .strip(); guard clauses / early return instead of deep nesting; 'if flag:' not 'if flag == True'; None as the default and create the list inside (mutable default); 'is' only for None; '//' when you mean whole-number result; f-strings for output; initialise accumulators before the loop; build a new list instead of mutating while iterating; write a function per sub-task; test empty/one/many. LIST COMPREHENSIONS: show a single 'optional' card only after Topic 6 mastery, framed as readable-for-simple-filters-only - CITS1401 assesses loops and Hermans' cognitive-load view argues against pushing terse idioms at novices. Include a printable summary (print CSS) since the app is static.

findings.detail: (1) EXPLAIN-THIS-ERROR PANEL - map exception type + message regex -> plain-English cause, typical fix, and the mistake id; highlight the traceback line in the editor (Monaco decorations); include Python 3.12's own 'Did you mean' suggestion. Enhanced error messages reduce repeated errors and teacher assistance (Becker; Kohn & Manaris: 95% of superficial errors fixed immediately). (2) EXAM MODE - CITS1401 has a competency test and a final exam; timed session, hints disabled, mixed formats, optional 'paper mode' with the Run button hidden so students practise tracing by hand; attempts tagged mode:'exam' so the report shows exam readiness separately. (3) SCRATCHPAD REPL - persistent Pyodide console pane in the editor (VS Code-like terminal), 'Try it' buttons on any snippet, and a step-through visualiser: run the snippet under sys.settrace and show a variable table per line (a lightweight notional machine, per Sorva/Python Tutor). (4) KEYBOARD SHORTCUTS - Cmd/Ctrl+Enter run, Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+Enter submit, 1-4 select MCQ option, H next hint tier, N next question, T theme, ? shortcut list. (5) WEEKLY PLAN - align topics to UWA 2026 teaching weeks (Sem 1: week 1 = 23 Feb ... week 12 = 18 May, study break 25 May, exams 1-8 Jun; Sem 2: week 1 = 20 Jul, week 6 = 24 Aug, break week, week 7 = 7 Sep ... week 12 = 12 Oct, study break 19 Oct, exams 26 Oct-2 Nov); a 'This week' card on the landing page with a user-adjustable week offset. (6) STREAKS AND DAILY GOAL - light-touch: credit for each day with >= 5 questions (the mechanism YeckehZaare et al. used), a streak counter without loss-aversion nagging; Denny (CHI 2013) found badges raised engagement without lowering quality. (7) CONFIDENCE RATING before reveal ('Sure' / 'Not sure') to detect lucky guesses and overconfidence - a cheap metacognitive signal for the report. (8) WORKED EXAMPLES WITH SUBGOAL LABELS at the start of each topic, faded worked -> completion -> write (Margulieux/Guzdial), plus a 'common mistakes in this topic' preview (erroneous examples). (9) PARAMETERISED VARIANTS - seedable numbers/lists so re-solving after seeing a solution is not rote; expected outputs computed by running the reference in Pyodide. (10) ACCESSIBILITY - keyboard-only navigation, reduced-motion respect, font size control, high-contrast tokens in both themes. (11) RUNTIME LOADING STRATEGY - Pyodide core is ~10 MB on first load; show a status pill ('Python runtime: loading / ready'), let MCQ/predict/Parsons work before it is ready, and consider a single-page shell (hash routing, topic data as JS files) so the runtime loads once per visit rather than per topic page - a deliberate deviation from the one-file-per-suite precedent.

findings.topic: Technical feasibility notes for the static, no-build stack
findings.detail: RUNTIME: Pyodide (CPython 3.12 compiled to WebAssembly; jsdelivr CDN, current line 314.0.x, e.g. https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/pyodide/v314.0.6/full/pyodide.js) gives real error messages, the 'ast' module for static checks, and sys.settrace for trace tables. Run it in a Web Worker; infinite loops are handled by a timeout that calls worker.terminate() and re-creates the worker (pyodide.setInterruptBuffer needs SharedArrayBuffer and COOP/COEP headers, unavailable on file:// or plain static hosts). input() is served via pyodide.setStdin({stdin: () => nextLine}) from a 'Program input' box or the test's stdin lines; stdout via setStdout({batched}). Web Workers cannot be created from file:// URLs in Chrome, so either serve locally (python -m http.server, the user has Python 3.12) or construct the worker from a Blob URL that importScripts the CDN. Skulpt (used by Runestone) is smaller but a Python-3 subset with different error messages - not recommended for a unit that assesses CPython behaviour. EDITOR: Monaco is literally VS Code's editor; the AMD build is on cdnjs (https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/monaco-editor/<ver>/min/vs/loader.js); AMD is deprecated from 0.53, so pin 0.52.x. Python has no Monaco language worker, so the cross-origin-worker restriction only matters for JS/TS features; basic tokenisation, themes (vs / vs-dark), bracket matching and keybindings work. CodeMirror 6 has no UMD build (needs a bundler); CodeMirror 5 is UMD on cdnjs if a lighter editor is preferred. AUTOGRADING SAFETY: run each submission in a fresh namespace (pyodide.runPython in a new dict globals), cap stdout length, cap time (3 s), and strip 'import' of os/sys/subprocess from student code only for user experience (Pyodide is already sandboxed: no filesystem access outside its virtual FS, no sockets). DESIGN SYSTEM: reuse the SQL hub tokens (dark default #0f0f0f / #171717 / #1e1e1e, accent #4ade80, warn #facc15, err #f87171, blue #60a5fa; light #f4f5f7 / #1a1d23; Inter + JetBrains Mono) and html[data-theme=light] override; map Monaco theme to the same tokens via monaco.editor.defineTheme.

recommendations: Adopt a 10-topic ladder aligned to CITS1401 lecture order (variables/expressions -> if/else -> while -> strings -> for/range -> lists -> functions -> dictionaries/tuples -> files/exceptions -> putting it together/recursion) and tag every question with week numbers for UWA 2026 Sem 1 (23 Feb-18 May) and Sem 2 (20 Jul-12 Oct).

Inside each topic, order formats up the tracing -> reading -> assembling/repairing -> writing hierarchy (predict-output and trace table first, Parsons/cloze/fix-the-bug next, write-a-function and refactor last); require one repair item and one write item for mastery so MCQ-only passes are impossible.

Implement the mistake taxonomy as a single JS/JSON catalogue keyed by mistake id with {category, topic, runtimeMatchers (exception type + message regex), astChecks (run in Pyodide via the ast module), testTags, distractorIds, explainText, patternCardId}; every detection channel writes the same id into the attempt log so the report is one aggregation.

Use Pyodide (CPython 3.12) in a Web Worker with a 3-second timeout + worker.terminate() for infinite loops, pyodide.setStdin for input() and stdin-driven program tests, and Python's own SyntaxError/'Did you mean' messages as the basis of the explain-this-error panel; compute expected outputs and trace tables by running reference code rather than hand-authoring them.

Use Monaco (pin 0.52.x AMD from cdnjs) themed with the SQL-hub tokens for the VS Code feel; consider a single-page shell so the ~10 MB runtime loads once, and let non-code formats work before it is ready.

Hints: four tiers (nudge, subgoal-labelled strategy, partial code, full solution + self-explanation prompt), dwell/attempt gated, one-submit MCQs, solution reveal after 2 failed attempts; log max tier, skims (<2 s), attempts-before-hint and solved-after-hint; score 1.0/0.9/0.75/0.5/0 by tier.

Unlock rule: all core items attempted, hint-weighted mastery >= 70%, plus one repair and one write solved; provide 'Test out' (5 mixed questions, >= 4/5, no hints) and a logged 'Unlock everything' override; show the rule on locked cards.

Spaced review scheduled per topic at +2/+7/+21 days, 3 questions per review, interleaving 2-3 due topics, a daily 'warm-up' card, credit for each day with >= 5 questions; reset interval on a failed review and surface it in the report.

Report: topic heatmap, mistake categories with repeat counts and median time-to-fix (weight conceptual/strategic above syntax slips), format x topic matrix with a generated diagnostic sentence, session trend sparklines, time-on-task rushed/stuck flags, exam-mode readiness, and rule-based pattern cards (PEP 8, enumerate, dict.get, with open, guard clauses, mutable-default fix) triggered by mistake counts, with list comprehensions gated as optional after list mastery.

Keep difficulty tags per question (easy/medium/hard by the 9-criterion rubric); derive scenario difficulty from its questions; add format, concepts, mistakes, core, week and expectedSec tags to the question schema.

Ship the extras with the best evidence-to-effort ratio first: explain-this-error panel, exam mode, scratchpad REPL with step-through variable table, keyboard shortcuts, weekly plan card, confidence rating, and JSON export/import of progress.
openQuestions: Will the app be opened via file:// (as the SQL hub presumably is) or served with 'python -m http.server'? Workers cannot be created from file:// in Chrome, so a Blob-URL worker or local server is required for Pyodide; this needs a quick test on the user's machine.

Should the build follow the one-HTML-file-per-topic precedent, or a single-page shell so the Pyodide runtime loads once per visit? The latter is recommended but deviates from the sibling project's architecture.
Monaco (heavier, exact VS Code look, AMD build deprecated after 0.52) vs CodeMirror 5 (lighter, UMD on cdnjs, less VS Code-like): which trade-off does the user prefer?

The exact CITS1401 week-by-week outline lives in the LMS; the lecture order used here comes from public lecture-slide listings. The user may want to confirm whether recursion and OOP/classes should be included at all.
Is the app single-user on one machine (localStorage only, as the SQL hub) or should progress sync across devices? Only export/import JSON is planned for now.
Does the user want free-text 'explain in plain English' items at all, given they cannot be autograded offline (self-check with model answer is the fallback)?
